transcript: 00:00:05 Jordan Hayes: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, with Priya who is our SE. We'll run through a quick SDK onramp for Python and TypeScript, plus auth patterns and the console. Avery, do you want to kick with your top success criteria?

00:00:28 Avery Cole: Yeah thanks, Jordan. Main things — we want a repeatable quickstart so our devs can get tokens and run local tests, also clear CI secret practices and, uh, importantly we need to understand private deploy options for PII workloads. Timeline is a 6 week pilot ideally.
00:00:52 Jordan Hayes: Perfect — Priya will handle the SDK and console bits. Quick note, feel free to interrupt with security questions — Lena I'm hoping you can flag anything big.

00:01:10 Priya Malhotra: Alright jumping in. First step, pip install redwood-sdk or npm i @redwood/inference. We'll show Python sample and then TS. I have a minimal app in the quickstart repo, link in the chat.
00:01:35 Samir Khan: Sorry can you say the package name again? I think I misheard — is it redwood-infer?

00:01:40 Priya Malhotra: It's redwood-sdk, sometimes older docs have different names — sorry about that, yes redwood-sdk for Py and @redwood/inference for TS. We updated the README to avoid that confusion.

00:02:05 Priya Malhotra: For auth, simplest is an API key you set as REDWOOD_API_KEY in env. For CI we recommend ephemeral CI keys via our console or Vault integration; don't store long-lived keys in code. We'll demo creating a sandbox key in the console now.

00:02:35 Jordan Hayes: Quick aside — on SSO, we integrate SAML and OIDC for console access. For programmatic access teams often pair SSO with short-lived keys via our token exchange flow. Lena, is that along the lines of what you need?
00:02:55 Lena Ortiz: Yes. Also want to confirm that keys can be scoped by route or model and rotated, and that audit logs capture token issuance.
00:03:09 Priya Malhotra: Yep — key scoping, rotation, and audit logs are all supported. We'll point you to the KMS notes for envelope encryption and HSM options.
00:03:30 Jordan Hayes: I'm going to share the sandbox org creation steps in the chat — you'll get an email invite. Priya you've got the console demo?

00:03:46 Priya Malhotra: Yep. Switching screens. First, top-level view: model catalog, routes, and usage. For Echo's use-case, we recommend a dedicated route for the service that will do summarization and one for embeddings. That lets you apply different batching and model choices per route.
00:04:20 Chris Vega: How do we set per-route cost controls? We want to avoid runaway spend during early testing.

00:04:29 Priya Malhotra: There's per-route throttling and token caps. Also Optimize will suggest batching configs and cheaper quantized variants if latency and quality trade-offs are acceptable. You can set an alert at, say, 300% of baseline spend and autoscale off on budget breach.
00:04:54 Samir Khan: When you say quantized variants, are those automatically served or do we need to pin model versions?

00:05:00 Priya Malhotra: You pin versions in the route. Optimize will recommend variants and you can do canary rollouts for evaluation. Automatic fallback is an option but we usually recommend staged rollout so you can verify quality.
00:05:24 Avery Cole: Ok that makes sense. Can you show the quickstart code for Python?

00:05:30 Priya Malhotra: Sure. Code snippet: from redwood_sdk import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.generate("Summarize this meeting...") — error handling pattern is in the README. For TS it's similar: import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood(process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY);
00:06:05 Samir Khan: Do you have examples for streaming vs sync calls? Our app prefers streaming to render partial UI.

00:06:12 Priya Malhotra: Yes, repo has streaming examples for SSE and Websocket SDK wrappers. Note that streaming has different timeout semantics and we recommend a small heartbeat window to keep connections alive on certain proxies.
00:06:36 Lena Ortiz: On encryption, is data encrypted at rest and in transit by default? How about customer-managed keys?

00:06:43 Jordan Hayes: In transit is TLS by default. At rest we use provider-managed encryption, and you can opt into customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for Private deployments. The SOC2 doc in the artifacts covers controls; Priya will send a short KMS integration note.

00:07:02 Priya Malhotra: I'm posting the KMS doc link now. For private/on-prem we hand over a private control plane and you can connect to your KMS. For VPC deployments there's an option to disable persistent logs if you need that for compliance.

00:07:23 Chris Vega: There's a lot there — for the pilot we probably will want the hosted sandbox with encrypted keys and route scoping, then evaluate private for prod. Timeline: start pilot in 6 weeks.

00:07:36 Jordan Hayes: Sounds good. Now quick demo of environment patterns: we recommend 3 envs (dev/stage/prod) with separate orgs or teams in the console, each with its own set of keys and RBAC. Sample k8s manifests and helm hooks are in the repo for on-prem or private infra teams.

00:08:05 Priya Malhotra: CI best practice: store REDWOOD_API_KEY in secret manager (GitHub Actions/GitLab/Circle) and use ephemeral key exchange on CI runners if you want tighter rotation. Avoid baking keys into images.
00:08:28 Samir Khan: For ephemeral keys — do we call an internal endpoint to exchange SSO token for a short-lived Redwood key?
00:08:35 Priya Malhotra: Exactly. We expose a token-exchange endpoint. The flow is documented and we've set up examples using OAuth client creds for service accounts.
00:08:50 Avery Cole: Any caveats for local dev? Our devs like simple env files but we want to avoid leaking keys.
00:08:56 Priya Malhotra: Use local dev keys that are scoped to a sandbox org and short-lived. Add .env to gitignore. The quickstart contains a script to rotate sandbox keys per dev every X days.

00:09:18 Jordan Hayes: Switching to console Optimize: it surfaces batching suggestions and shows token breakdowns per route — that helps pick model variants. For example, if you feed many short requests, Optimize might recommend more aggressive batching to reduce unit cost.
00:09:45 Chris Vega: Does Optimize also flag quality regressions if we change models?

00:09:50 Priya Malhotra: Yes, we tie evals/prompt sets to routes so you can detect regression alerts when a model or quantization change affects outputs. We also keep a diff view for outputs across rollouts.
00:10:10 Lena Ortiz: On audit logs — do we get token-level usage? We need traceability for compliance audits.

00:10:17 Jordan Hayes: We provide token-level breakdowns, request ids, and tracing hooks you can pipe into your SIEM. For Private, you can retain logs within your region with a configurable retention window.

00:10:40 Samir Khan: Ok, let's dig into an integration question: our backend is node services that batch user requests — what's the recommended concurrency strategy to keep latency under 300ms for summarization?

00:10:52 Priya Malhotra: For short summaries, use per-request streaming and low-latency model variants; set a small batch window (20–50ms) and continuous batching. If you need sub-300ms p95, we'll recommend a dedicated pool with pinned GPUs in Dedicated offering. We can run a microbench with your typical payloads to baseline.
00:11:25 Avery Cole: That microbench would be helpful. Can Redwood run it against our sample dataset?
00:11:30 Jordan Hayes: Yes, we can sign an NDA if needed, and run a baseline. We'll want a small sample and a test script. Add that to the next steps.

00:11:48 Priya Malhotra: Quick note on errors — we return structured error codes. Our client SDK has retry helpers and idempotency keys patterns in the repo. If you hit rate limits, the SDK surfaces that and suggests backoff.
00:12:10 Chris Vega: Any known gotchas with proxies or corp networks? We have strict egress rules and some internal proxies drop long-lived SSE.

00:12:18 Priya Malhotra: Right — SSE can be flaky behind certain proxies. We provide websocket fallback and chunked-stream alternatives. In an extreme, you can use our gateway in VPC mode to avoid public egress.
00:12:38 Samir Khan: For pilot, we may want webhook-based async patterns so UI isn't blocked. Does Redwood support async job patterns?
00:12:44 Priya Malhotra: Yes, we have async job endpoints and callbacks, plus a polling option. The SDK includes a helper to manage job lifecycle.
00:13:02 Jordan Hayes: We're at 13 minutes in, we can switch to a short live quickstart run — Priya will walk through the repo in a dev environment and show the pip/npm install and local run.

00:13:18 Priya Malhotra: Opening the repo. First open quickstart/python/README.md — run python -m venv venv; pip install -r requirements.txt; export REDWOOD_API_KEY=...; python examples/summarize.py. For TS: cd quickstart/ts; npm i; export REDWOOD_API_KEY=...; node dist/index.js.
00:13:52 Samir Khan: The Python readme mentions a 'fast' model flag — is that a model name?

00:13:58 Priya Malhotra: It's a shim in the client that selects a latency-optimized model alias. The actual model name is in the catalog and may be something like redwood-medium-q4. We'll include a mapping table in the README.
00:14:18 Chris Vega: Do we need to change any CORS settings for web clients calling Redwood endpoints?

00:14:24 Priya Malhotra: If you call from browser directly you need to use the browser-specific key flow and CORS settings in the console — we generally recommend server-for-server calls with the key in the backend.
00:14:44 Jordan Hayes: Quick recap of compliance bullets: SOC2 summary shared, KMS/HSM options for private, audit logs available, RBAC and SSO for console. Lena — any follow-ups?
00:14:58 Lena Ortiz: I'd like the threat model doc and a short write-up on data residency in VPC mode. Also a checklist for penetration test scope if we move private.
00:15:10 Jordan Hayes: Noted. We'll add 'threat model' to the artifacts we send.

00:15:22 Priya Malhotra: A couple more specifics — for VPC/private we ship a control plane that you host in your account; we've done air-gapped installs before but that takes more lead time. For the pilot, hosted sandbox + VPC peering is usually fastest.
00:15:44 Samir Khan: Lead time? If we decide private, how long to get infra up?
00:15:50 Priya Malhotra: Depends on network approvals, but typically 4–8 weeks for first private deploy including KMS setup and compliance checks. We'll scope that in the follow-up.
00:16:10 Avery Cole: Ok good. Let's record the immediate asks: sandbox keys + quickstart, SOC2 and KMS notes, microbench proposal. Jordan will send invite for scoping meeting next week.
00:16:25 Jordan Hayes: Yep — action items as discussed. Any final questions before we wrap?
00:16:32 Chris Vega: One minor — do you charge for test tokens in sandbox?
00:16:36 Jordan Hayes: Sandbox is covered under free credits for the pilot; we'll detail cost expectations once we have baseline metrics from the microbench.
00:16:47 Priya Malhotra: I'll also add an example GitHub Actions workflow that exchanges a service account for ephemeral keys and shows how to run quickstart in CI.
00:16:59 Samir Khan: Great, that will help our infra team. Thanks.
00:17:10 Jordan Hayes: Alright thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items in the chat. Meeting notes and links will be in the calendar invite. Have a good one.
